title: Research
text:
2017-Present - LTER Camera Trap Wildlife Monitoring Network NPHK

Long-term Infrastructure


A continuous camera trap monitoring initiative collecting long-term spatial and temporal data on mammal populations in National Park Hoge Kempen. The network operated under a systematic random sampling design from 2017 to 2020 and has since transitioned into a stratified random sampling design. The dataset has already supported multiple published scientific studies, cross-institutional collaborations, and student thesis projects and internships.
 Access 2017–2020 Open Dataset on GBIF



Funders:










2024-2029 - Expanding Management Strategy Evaluation ((G)MSE) for Multi-Species Wildlife Management and Conservation

PhD Project


Wildlife management decisions often target a single species, overlooking complex species interactions and conflicting management goals. The PhD project of Imke Tomsin focuses on advancing the Generalised Management Strategy Evaluation (GMSE) mechanistic modelling framework to account for multiple interacting species and multi-objective decision-making in complex social-ecological systems.



Supervisors: Prof. Dr. Natalie Beenaerts (Hasselt University), Dr. ir. Jim Casaer (INBO), Prof. Dr. Nils Bunnefeld & Dr. Brad Duthie (University of Stirling), Prof. Dr. Herwig Leirs (University of Antwerp)


Funding: FWO PhD Fellowship Fundamental Research (Grant number 1120326N)

title: Wim Kuypers
text: I am a PhD researcher in environmental sciences focusing on human-wildlife interactions in highly visited protected areas. My research explores how different forms of human recreation influence spatiotemporal behaviour of wildlife, combining large-scale camera trap data with statistical modelling and human-tracking data sources such as social media-derived recreation data. Outside of my research, I am happiest when I can spend time outdoors and with friends. I enjoy hiking, camping, fishing, eating nice food, and simply going on adventures and exploring new places.

title: Field Research Centre
text:
Who are we?
The Field Research Centre (FRC) is the ecological field station of Hasselt University, positioned at the gateway to Nationaal Park Hoge Kempen. Operating within the ProtEct research group of the Centre for Environmental Sciences (CMK), our research ranges from long-term ecosystem monitoring to fundamental and applied studies on wildlife, biodiversity, human-nature interactions, and global change.
We place a strong emphasis on national and international collaboration, student training, and science communication. Whether you are looking to partner on research, join our team, or simply explore our work, we welcome you to get in touch!

Explore Our Research
Meet the Team

title: Field Research Centre
text:
Research Focus


🔍 Long-Term Ecological Monitoring
Part of the European eLTER network, collecting data across Nationaal Park Hoge Kempen using camera traps and IoT sensors.


🦇 Fundamental & Evolutionary Ecology
Conducting empirical research on ecological traits, stress tolerance, and community structures across diverse ecosystems.


🚶 Human-Nature Interactions
Investigating how human density, recreation, and habitat fragmentation impact wildlife dynamics and biodiversity in complex, multi-use landscapes.


🐗 Mechanistic Modelling
Developing predictive models to evaluate management strategies and support evidence-based wildlife and wildfire management and conservation.

🚗 Car
Take Exit 33 on the E314 highway (Brussels – Aachen). Follow the signs for ‘Maasmechelen Leisure Valley’ along the route that runs alongside the canal for several kilometers.
Continue following the main road through three roundabouts until you see signage directing you toward ‘PARKING EUROSCOOP’ and ‘TERHILLS’. Park your vehicle in this designated area.
From the parking lot, walk approximately 300 meters through the historic French Garden. You will find the Field Research Centre located on your left side.

title: Eliana Muccio
text:
I am a PhD candidate at the Université de Namur and Hasselt University, where I am working on a project that examines human–wolf interactions in Belgium and explore how humans and wolves can coexist in such densely populated, agricultural landscapes. My research takes an interdisciplinary approach, combining public attitude surveys, media discourse analysis, and stakeholder engagement with local actors. Adopting such methodology, my aim is to develop evidence-based, socially inclusive strategies that bridge the gap between science, policy, and society.
Before starting my PhD, I completed an MSc in Global Wildlife Health and Conservation and a BSc in Zoology at the University of Bristol, where I conducted research on topics ranging from the impacts of marine tourism on bottlenose dolphins to sustainable rice cultivation practices in Madagascar. I also gained practical experience in conservation and fundamental conceptual knowledge of political ecology and human-nature coexistence through roles with the Convivial Conservation Centre, coordinating international projects and communication strategies aimed at spreading the word about Convivial conservation strategies. Through my work, I try to combine different social science perspectives and concepts to better understand human–wildlife interactions and contribute to conservation strategies that are both scientifically robust and socially inclusive.

title: Robbe Van Wassenhove
text: I study small mammals, with a primary focus on bats, in Belgian Limburg’s national parks and surrounding cross-border regions. My research focuses on generating long-term, fundamental data on small-mammal populations and their habitat use, as well as evaluating the effectiveness of nature restoration and landscape connectivity measures in supporting the favourable conservation status of these ecologically important species.

title: Siebe Indestege
text: My research focuses on the methodology behind long-term ecological monitoring, especially in wildlife monitoring, to support decision-making in wildlife management conservation. On the one side, I am interested in the possibilities of camera trap sampling designs modifications to allow multiple specific research questions to be investigated within one long-term monitoring project. On the other hand, I am inspired by modern GPS-trackers embedded in an IoT-network allowing broad-scale, budget-efficient, and highly technological data gathering.

title: Prof. Dr. Yanet Cruz Portorreal
text: My research focuses on coastal socio-ecological systems, with particular emphasis on mangrove ecosystems, climate change, carbon sequestration and resilience. I am interested in understanding the interactions between ecological processes and human activities in coastal areas, and in developing interdisciplinary approaches that can support climate-change mitigation, adaptation and sustainable coastal management. My current work combines socio-ecological systems thinking, integrated coastal management and DPSIR-based approaches to analyse drivers of environmental change, interactions between people and ecosystems, knowledge and information flows, and opportunities for strengthening resilience. I am particularly interested in linking ecological evidence, local and traditional knowledge, and stakeholder perspectives to inform more context-sensitive and actionable coastal management strategies, especially in the Cuban context.
